extracted.intended_audience: washington post journalists, editors, contributors, and newsroom staff
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial and ethical standards for reporting, sourcing, corrections, and audience engagement at The Washington Post. Covers mission/principles, conflicts of interest, verification, source attribution, corrections, and conduct (including social media) for newsroom staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission statement — The Seven Principles for the Conduct of a Newspaper
rubrics_metrics.description: The mission is defined by seven principles written by Eugene Meyer (1935) that articulate the newspaper’s responsibilities to tell the truth, tell all the truth it can learn, observe decencies, be fit reading for young and old, be duty-bound to readers and the public rather than owners’ private interests, be prepared to sacrifice material fortunes for the public good, and not be the ally of any special interest but remain fair and wholesome in outlook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original wording: “The first mission of a newspaper is to tell the truth as nearly as the truth may be ascertained.” The seven principles are intended as guiding moral precepts for all news coverage and editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics policy (living document)
rubrics_metrics.description: These policies are meant to guide Washington Post journalism and are a synthesis of Post policies; they are described as a “living document” that will be modified and updated and are not meant to be comprehensive or to establish hard and fast rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance emphasizes discretion: because circumstances vary, the guidelines should not be understood as covering every situation. Journalists should consult editors/legal as needed and adapt principles to case-by-case circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post is pledged to avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance of conflicts wherever possible and has stringent policies (often more restrictive than private business practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific rules/examples: "We pay our own way." Accept no gifts from news sources, no free trips, avoid preferential treatment; exceptions are few/obvious (occasional meals). Free admissions to events not free to public are prohibited except limited press/critic exceptions, with payment arrangements whenever possible. No payment/honoraria/expenses from governments, government-funded organizations, political groups, or from persons/organizations a reporter covers. Avoid accepting money from lobbyists or those trying to influence issues covered. Avoid entanglement with subjects of coverage; private behavior that brings discredit should be avoided. Avoid active involvement in partisan causes, community affairs or demonstrations that could compromise impartiality. Disclose business and professional ties of household/family members to department heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters and editors are committed to fairness — which includes completeness, relevance, honesty, and giving subjects opportunity to respond to assertions about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No story is fair if it omits significant facts, includes irrelevant information at expense of significant facts, misleads the reader, or covers individuals/organizations without giving them opportunity to address claims. Fairness involves diligently seeking comment and taking it genuinely into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste and decency
rubrics_metrics.description: Respect society’s concepts of taste and decency; avoid prurience and avoid profanities/obscenities unless essential to a story’s meaning and then only with executive/management approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If content may offend but has legitimate news value, editors should use visual and/or text warnings (example: warning before linking to graphic images). Do not link to sites that aid or abet illegal activity; consult Legal if unsure whether a site falls under this rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion separation and labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Separation of news columns from editorial pages is solemn and complete; analysis/ perspective/ opinion/review must be plainly labeled to serve readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels defined: Analysis = interpretation of news based on evidence and data; Perspective = discussion with a point of view including first-person narratives; Opinion = columns/blogs in Opinions section; Review = critic’s assessment of services/products/artistic works. News may include analysis/commentary if plainly labeled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington Post journalists must protect professional integrity on social networks; journalists are always Washington Post journalists in both reporting and personal lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social-media accounts reflect on newsroom credibility. Even personal/informal expression should preserve reputation for excellence, fairness and independence. Consider every comment/link as public information. Refrain from posting anything that could objectively be perceived as reflecting political, racial, sexist, religious or other bias or favoritism.

rubrics_metrics.name: National and community interest standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post is concerned with national and community interest and believes these are best served by widest possible dissemination of information; claims of national/community interest do not automatically equate with those interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors/reporters should evaluate asserted national/community interest critically (an official’s claim is not determinative) and favor dissemination that serves the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: A journalist’s role and identity honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should remain in the audience (stagehand rather than star) and should not misrepresent their identity or occupation in gathering news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not portray oneself as police, physicians or other professions; identify as Washington Post reporters. Reporting should be honorable and defensible publicly. Do not use pseudonyms or mislead readers about identities of people in stories; decisions to provide less than full names require editor participation and explanation to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and fact‑checking responsibilities and review structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Washington Post reporters have primary responsibility for reporting, writing and fact‑checking their stories; stories are subject to review by one or more editors as part of a multi-level review and editing structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors involved may include assignment editors (department heads/deputies/assistant editors), multiplatform/copy editors, and senior editors who oversee digital and print presentation. The number of editors and extent of review varies by complexity, sensitivity, and time pressure. Digital presentation (headlines, alerts, newsletters) may involve platform editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity is core to Washington Post journalism: reporting accurately requires engaging a variety of voices as interviewees and writers, striving for staff that reflects diverse backgrounds and life experiences, and seeking feedback from varied voices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post submits staff diversity data to the American Society of News Editors and encourages reporters to expand their universe of sources to include women, younger people, people of color, unconventional thinkers and ordinary citizens affected by stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership structure disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post discloses its ownership: currently owned by Jeffrey P. Bezos; Post founded in 1877.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure of ownership is presented as part of transparency about the news organization’s structure and potential interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections policy — promptness, transparency, and standards for corrections/clarifications/editor’s notes
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post strives for nimble, accurate and complete reporting and seeks to be promptly responsive in correcting errors on digital platforms and in print; corrections should tell readers what was wrong and what is correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Updating a digital report: time stamps signal developing stories and updates do not always need notes unless a significant mistake is corrected. Use a correction, clarification or editor’s note when correcting significant mistakes. Corrections: publish promptly and explain the change. Clarification: rewrite unclear language while facts are correct and add clarification notice (also used when initial failure to seek comment is rectified). Editor’s Note: used when correction calls into question entire substance, raises significant ethical matters, or addresses unmet standards — requires senior editor approval. Additional rules: when readers point out errors in comments, indicate in comments when corrected; send alerts to correct erroneous alerts; correct social network errors on that platform; do not attribute blame to individual reporters/editors but may note production problems or trusted-source errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take‑down (unpublish) requests
rubrics_metrics.description: The editorial policy is not to grant take‑down/unpublish requests as a general rule; requests should be vetted at the highest level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subject claims inaccuracy, investigate and if necessary publish a correction. Consider follow-up coverage if fairness demands. Do not remove article as though it never existed. Takedown review may be considered when published personal data puts a person at risk of physical harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on sources — transparency and preference for named sources
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post is committed to disclosing to readers the sources of information in its stories to the maximum possible extent to make reporting transparent and earn reader trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Named sources are vastly preferred to unnamed sources. Reporters should press sources to go on the record and should seek to tell readers why unnamed sources deserve confidence (provide context such as the source’s role or relationship to events). Original reporting is valued; reporters should try to see as much of the story firsthand when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential sources and criteria for granting anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: Granting anonymity to sources should be done reluctantly and not casually; in some circumstances anonymity is necessary (e.g., to expose corruption) but should be carefully weighed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer at least two independent sources for factual information that depends on confidential informants; prefer sources with firsthand knowledge; relevant documents can serve as a second source. Some single-source situations may be published only after deliberation by executive editor, managing editor, and department head — decision depends on source reliability and basis for information. Editors should know the identity of unnamed sources so they and reporters can assess appropriateness; resist sources who demand withholding identity from editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution and original reporting (truthfulness about information origin)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be truthful about the source of information; facts and quotations not from our reporting must be attributed. Distinguish what the reporter saw from what was obtained from other outlets or sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Total attribution is required for material from other media. Plagiarism is prohibited. If reporter was not present at a scene, the story should make that clear and attribute assertions about events to witnesses or other sources. Reconstructed exchanges based on witnesses must be transparently attributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground rules and definitions of attribution terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear ground rules must be established at interview start; The Post defines on the record, on background/not for attribution, deep background, and off the record, and instructs reporters how to use these categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On the record = attributable to the source by name. On background/not for attribution = attributable descriptively (e.g., "a police department official"); press for maximum revelation and useful attribution. Deep background = information usable but not attributed — to be avoided where possible. Off the record = traditionally means information cannot be used; be cautious and clarify meaning with sources who misuse the term. Establish ground rules verbally (preferably on tape) and start interviews with presumption of on the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quoting sources and sharing drafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective in quoting is to capture words and intended meaning accurately; sources may not be allowed to change quotes after the fact, and sharing entire drafts with sources is generally prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow sources to change what was said in an original interview. Reading back quotes to ensure accuracy is sometimes used, but allowing a source to change an original quote is not permitted (a source may add to a quotation and that addition can be explained to readers). Some reporters may share sections of stories with sources to check technical points, but sharing entire drafts prior to publication is against policy except with extremely rare permission from the Executive or Managing Editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert sources and breadth of voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a broad range of expert voices and avoid dependence on the same academics or public figures for reactions and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek new specialists (women, younger people, people of color, unconventional thinkers), and include ordinary citizens affected by events (students, teachers, employees) to reflect readership and general population. Make effort to expand source universe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader engagement and feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: The Post welcomes reader contributions and interaction (comments, live chats, letters, op-eds); reader scrutiny often improves journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most articles offer comment sections and live chats; reporters/editors encouraged to participate based on preference. Commenters must keep tone civil and follow Discussion and Submission Guidelines; moderation team handles offensive comments. Audience engagement team should note corrections in comment threads. Letters and op-eds have submission channels; readers can contact the reader representative for questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: No linking to sites that aid or abet illegal activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid linking to websites that facilitate illegal activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unsure whether a site aids/abets illegal activity, consult the Legal Department. Even when linking externally, include warnings when content may be offensive or graphic.
